title: You Think Quiet Dry Rooms Always Boost Memory, Yet Scuba Divers Remembered More Underwater
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Godden & Baddeley (1975): Scuba Divers 20 Feet Underwater — Why Recall Jumps 46% When Your Surroundings Match, grounded in D. R. Godden, A. D. Baddeley (1975) (British Journal of Psychology). Empirical findings show that commercial deep-sea oil divers off 1970s Scotland kept complaining to psychologist Alan Baddeley that observations they memorized clearly on the seabed vanished the moment they climbed back onto the deck boat. Baddeley and diving colleague *Duncan Godden (1975, British Journal of Psychology) took 18 scuba divers to the cold waters of Oban, Scotland to run a pristine 2×2 crossover*.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Divers listened twice to lists of 36 unrelated words either DRY sitting on the rocky shore in diving gear OR WET hovering 20 feet (~6 meters) underwater breathing compressed air, then waited 4 minutes and wrote down every word they could remember either in the SAME environment or the OPPOSITE environment (using weighted plastic formica slates and pencils underwater!).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- D. R. Godden, A. D. Baddeley (1975). CONTEXT‐DEPENDENT MEMORY IN TWO NATURAL ENVIRONMENTS: ON LAND AND UNDERWATER. British Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1975.tb01468.x
- Duncan Godden, Alan Baddeley (1980). When does context influence recognition memory? British Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1980.tb02735.x
- Steven M. Smith, Edward Vela, John E. Williamson (1988). Shallow input processing does not induce environmental context-dependent recognition. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03330115
